summary: Defines the WebFinger protocol, which uses ordinary HTTP to discover information about people or other entities identified by a URI, such as an account or email address that is not itself a usable locator. Results are returned as JSON Resource Descriptors.

plainLanguage.summary: You know someone's email address and want to find out more about them. WebFinger is a lookup that answers politely.

questions: how to look up info for an email address
what is the webfinger well-known path
what is a json resource descriptor
how does the webfinger rel parameter work
subtitle: A plain HTTPS lookup that turns an account or email-style identifier into a JSON description of links and facts about it.

tldr.problem: Identifiers such as account names and email addresses are not usable locators, so there is no standard way to find information about the person or thing behind them.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends an HTTPS GET to the well-known path /.well-known/webfinger with a resource parameter naming the URI, and the server returns a JSON Resource Descriptor listing aliases, properties and links.
tldr.outcome: WebFinger gives applications a shared lookup mechanism, but each application must define its own URI scheme, properties and link relation types, and the data is meant to be static and public.

today: RFC 7033 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of WebFinger.

sections.title: What WebFinger Is For
sections.content:
WebFinger discovers information about people or other entities on the Internet that are identified by a URI, using standard HTTP methods over a secure transport. It is aimed at URIs that cannot be used as locators on their own, such as account or email URIs.

For a person, the result might include a personal profile address, an identity service, a telephone number or a preferred avatar. For other things, such as a printer, it might say that the printer can print in color on A4 paper, or give the physical location of a server.

The information is meant to be static. The RFC says WebFinger is not intended to return dynamic values such as the temperature of a CPU or the current toner level in a laser printer.
sections.plainLanguage: WebFinger is a lookup for finding out more about something when all you have is its name, like finding someone's profile page from their email address. It is for things that stay the same, not things that change every minute.

sections.title: Making a WebFinger Query
sections.content:
A WebFinger request is an HTTPS GET to a well-known URI whose path is /.well-known/webfinger. The resource MUST NOT be served over any other scheme such as HTTP. The query string MUST contain a resource parameter, exactly once, holding the URI being asked about, and MAY contain one or more rel parameters.

Each parameter value is percent-encoded, and the characters = and & inside values are encoded too. The client MUST NOT insert spaces, and the order of parameters does not matter.

The host matters. If the query target has a host portion, the query SHOULD go to that same host, unless the client has out-of-band instructions to use another. If the target has no host, the client picks a host using other information.

If resource is missing or malformed, the server MUST say the request is bad. If the server has no information for the value, it MUST say it could not match the request. A server MAY redirect, but only to an https URI, and the client must validate the certificate again. Servers can also send cache validators and expiration times.

If HTTPS fails for any reason, including an invalid certificate or a 4xx or 5xx response, the client MUST treat the query as failed and MUST NOT retry over plain HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on a fixed, well-known door at the website and say which name you are asking about. The door only opens for a secure knock, and if it is locked you may not try a side window.

sections.title: The JSON Resource Descriptor
sections.content:
The reply is a JSON Resource Descriptor (JRD), served as application/jrd+json. It was introduced in RFC 6415 and is based on the XRD format. A JRD is a JSON object with four members: subject, aliases, properties and links. A client MUST ignore any unknown member rather than treat it as an error.

  • subject is a URI naming the entity described. It SHOULD be present and MAY differ from the requested resource, for example when an account moves or the server prefers a canonical form.
  • aliases is an optional array of URIs that identify the same entity.
  • properties is an optional object whose names are URIs and whose values are strings or null.
  • links is an optional array of link relation objects.

Each link object has rel (required, exactly one registered relation type or one URI), and optional type (a media type), href (a target URI), titles and properties. The titles object is keyed by language tag, or und when the language is unknown. The order of links MAY be read as an order of preference.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a small card with the name, other names for the same thing, a few facts, and a list of links. Each link says what kind of link it is and where it points.

sections.title: Filtering with the rel Parameter
sections.content:
A client MAY add one or more rel parameters to ask for only certain link relation types. When the server supports this, only matching links stay in the links array; if nothing matches, the array is empty or absent. Everything else in the JRD, including aliases and properties, is still returned.

Servers SHOULD support rel. A server that does not MUST ignore it and answer as if it were absent, so a client must not assume the links array contains only what it asked for. The RFC notes that the parameter can reduce processing and bandwidth when there are many links.

The RFC's first example is a web site that wants only the OpenID Connect provider for carol@example.com. It asks for acct:carol@example.com with a single rel and gets back one link.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for only one kind of link is like asking the librarian for just the cookbooks. A busy librarian might hand you the whole shelf anyway, so you check what you got.

sections.title: Browsers, Access Control and Hosting
sections.content:
Web browsers apply same-origin rules, so servers MUST include the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing). Servers SHOULD use the least restrictive setting, which allows any domain (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *), but a server on an intranet with sensitive company information SHOULD NOT allow any domain and should use a more restrictive value.

Access to a WebFinger resource may require authentication, and a server MAY give different answers to different clients, for example showing employee picture links only inside a corporate network. Those policy decisions are outside the scope of the RFC.

Hosted services: a domain owner can let a third party run WebFinger, much like pointing MX records at a mail host. The server MUST then answer with a redirect that carries a Location header. The RFC's example redirects a query for acct:alice@example.com to wf.example.net with a 307 status.
sections.plainLanguage: A website can say who is allowed to peek at its answers. A company can also have another company answer the questions for it, by pointing visitors to the other company's desk.

sections.title: Defining WebFinger Applications
sections.content:
WebFinger itself defines only the query syntax, the JRD format, security requirements and hosting. It does not say which properties or link relation types to expect for a given URI. Any application built on it MUST specify those details in its own document.

  • The application MUST specify the URI scheme or schemes, and what forms the URIs take. Examples in the RFC are the acct scheme for accounts and web page URLs for copyright information.
  • If a URI has no host, or the host should not be used, the application MUST define how the host is resolved, possibly with a default host in the client.
  • It MUST define the URIs used for properties and the valid values, and each link with its relation type, media type, properties and titles.

Clients SHOULD ignore properties or links they do not fully understand and SHOULD NOT report an error. A simple token used as a link relation type MUST be registered with IANA, and defined properties MUST be registered too.
sections.plainLanguage: WebFinger is the postal system, not the letters. Each use of it has to decide what the letters say and how to read them.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
HTTPS is REQUIRED so information is not modified in transit, and clients MUST verify the server certificate and accept a response only if it is valid. WebFinger also inherits the security considerations of CORS.

On privacy, a service that exposes personal data via WebFinger MUST give users an interface to choose which data elements are exposed. It MUST NOT publish personal data unless the person explicitly authorized it. The RFC warns about sharing location information, and says easy access to user information was a design goal, not a limitation.

On abuse, a query can reveal whether an email address is valid, and linked data could help spammers or phishers. Server implementers are RECOMMENDED to mitigate abuse, and the RFC names rate-limiting by IP address as one option. Clients are strongly advised not to query automatically, for example for every sender of incoming mail, unless the user authorizes it, since that would tell a spammer the user just checked email. Finally, the data may be false or manipulated, and HTTPS cannot fix incorrect data supplied by the server.
sections.plainLanguage: Because anyone can ask, people must choose what goes on the card. Visitors should also be careful, since a card can be wrong and some questions tell the other side who is asking.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the webfinger suffix in the Well-Known URIs registry, with the IETF as change controller. It also registers the media type application/jrd+json, with no charset parameter because JSON already defines its character encoding, and the file extension jrd.

It reuses the existing Link Relation Types registry for relation types used by WebFinger applications, and creates a new WebFinger Properties registry. A registration uses a template with Property Identifier, Link Type, Description, Reference and an optional Notes field.

Properties are registered with Specification Required after review by Designated Experts, with discussion on a public mailing list encouraged first. The review is normally expected to take on the order of two to four weeks.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC puts the special door name and the answer format on official lists so nobody reuses them. It also starts a new list for the kinds of facts that can appear on the card.

data.title: OpenID Connect issuer lookup
data.code:
GET /.well-known/webfinger?
       resource=acct%3Acarol%40example.com&
       rel=http%3A%2F%2Fopenid.net%2Fspecs%2Fconnect%2F1.0%2Fissuer
       HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Content-Type: application/jrd+json

{
  "subject" : "acct:carol@example.com",
  "links" :
  [
    {
      "rel" : "http://openid.net/specs/connect/1.0/issuer",
      "href" : "https://openid.example.com"
    }
  ]
}
